mainTopic: Doubled verbs in the Torah that teach 'מכל מקום' (in any case), and the finder's pay and conditions made before a בית דין when returning a lost item.
overview: First the גמרא finishes explaining why the Torah needed separate פסוקים for השבת אבידה, פריקה and טעינה. With פריקה and טעינה the owner is standing with his animal, so we might have thought there is no duty to help. Next comes a ברייתא listing doubled verbs (like מות יומת, הכה תכה, השב תשיב, חבל תחבל, פתח תפתח, נתן תתן, הענק תעניק, העבט תעביטנו). Each doubled verb widens a law to apply 'מכל מקום,' in any case. Along the way the גמרא explains why two collateral פסוקים are needed: one is for a day garment and one for a night garment. For רבי אלעזר בן עזריה and רבי שמעון, who reject some of these rules, the doubling is just normal speech: דברה תורה כלשון בני אדם. The גמרא then returns to the משנה. A finder who stopped working is paid like a פועל בטל, which אביי explains as an idle worker from his own kind of work. Finally, the משנה lets the finder set a condition before a בית דין. This leads to a story where רב ספרא split up a partnership in front of only two people, and רבה בר רב הונא required three. His alternative option continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why loading and unloading needed their own verses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends its צריכותא. With פריקה and טעינה the owner is present with his animal, so we might have thought there is no duty to help. That is why the Torah had to write them separately.
steps.simpleTranslation: But these two, where the owner is with the animal, I would have said no. So it was necessary to write them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an explanation of why the Torah needed to write several similar מצוות. It shows that השבת אבידה alone would not have taught us פריקה and טעינה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a lost item, the owner is not there to look after his property, so the Torah tells you to step in. With פריקה and טעינה, the owner is standing right next to his animal. So we might have thought he can handle it himself and you need not help. That difference is why the Torah needed separate פסוקים, and the conclusion is 'צְרִיכָא', all of them are needed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary; the גמרא's word for showing that each of several similar sources is needed
I would say no (we might have thought the law doesn't apply)

steps.whatToRemember: A צריכותא shows that each similar מצוה teaches something the others could not. Here, the owner being present with his animal is what makes פריקה and טעינה different from השבת אבידה.
steps.confusionAlert: 'הָנֵי תַּרְתֵּי' does not mean 'two people.' It means the two מצוות of unloading and loading the animal.

phrases.english: But these two
phrases.notes: He means the two מצוות of unloading and loading an animal.

phrases.english: where its owner is with it,
I would say no.
phrases.notes: Meaning: I might have thought there's no duty to help, since the owner is right there.

phrases.english: It is necessary.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל הָנֵי תַּרְתֵּי דְּאִיתֵאּ לְמָרַהּ בַּהֲדַהּ, אֵימָא לָא. צְרִיכָא.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the צריכותא that began before this section of the daf.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All the פסוקים are needed. Since the owner is present for פריקה and טעינה, those could not be learned from השבת אבידה.

steps.title: A murderer may be executed by any available method
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the doubled verb 'מות יומת' means a רוצח must be executed even if the usual death penalty (the sword) cannot be carried out.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The one who struck shall surely be put to death.' From this alone I would only know he is killed with the death written for him. How do we know that if you can't kill him that way, you may kill him with any method you can? The verse says 'מות יומת', meaning in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a series of doubled verbs. This is the first one: the doubled 'מות יומת' said about a רוצח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a רוצח gets the specific death penalty the Torah assigns him. The ברייתא asks what happens if that method is not possible. The doubled verb teaches that the goal is that he be put to death in any case, so another method is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: He shall surely be put to death (a doubled verb)
I only know (the basic, limited meaning)
In any case / in any way

steps.confusionAlert: This does not change the normal death penalty for a רוצח. The doubled verb only covers the case where the normal method can't be done.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a pattern: a doubled verb (מקור plus regular verb) often widens a law to 'מכל מקום,' in any case.

phrases.english: 'The one who struck shall surely be put to death,'
I have only
the death that is written for him.
From where do we know that if you are unable
to kill him with the death written for him,
you are permitted to kill him with any death
with which you are able to kill him?
The verse says: 'shall surely be put to death,'
in any case.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״מוֹת יוּמַת הַמַּכֶּה״, אֵין לִי אֶלָּא בְּמִיתָה הַכְּתוּבָה בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא listing doubled verbs. It connects to the doubled verbs (like השב תשיבם) the גמרא was discussing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a רוצח cannot be killed by his written death penalty, he may be killed by any available method, learned from the doubled 'מות יומת'.

steps.title: The people of an idolatrous city may be struck by any method
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: the doubled 'הכה תכה' said about an עיר הנדחת teaches that if they can't be executed the written way, any available method may be used.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You shall surely strike.' From this alone I would only know they are struck the way written for them. How do we know that if you can't kill them that way, you may strike them with any striking you can? The verse says 'הכה תכה', meaning in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second example in the ברייתא. It uses the same pattern for the doubled verb 'הכה תכה' said about an עיר הנדחת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah commands striking the people of an עיר הנדחת with the sword. The doubled verb widens this: if the sword can't be used, any other effective way is allowed. The structure is word-for-word the same as the רוצח case, just applied to a group.

keyTerms.meaning: You shall surely strike (a doubled verb)
A city that was led into idol worship

phrases.english: 'You shall surely strike,'
phrases.notes: דברים 13:16. This is about an עיר הנדחת.

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא בְּהַכָּאָה הַכְּתוּבָה בָּהֶן,
phrases.english: I have only the striking written for them,
From where do we know that if you are unable
to kill them with the striking written for them,
you are permitted to strike them
with any striking that you are able to?
The verse says: 'You shall surely strike,'
in any case.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״הַכֵּה תַכֶּה״, אֵין לִי אֶלָּא בְּהַכָּאָה הַכְּתוּבָה בָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second example in the same ברייתא, following the same pattern as מות יומת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The people of an עיר הנדחת may be executed by any available method if the written method can't be done, learned from 'הכה תכה'.

steps.title: Returning collateral even if taken without the court's permission
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's third example: the doubled 'השב תשיב' teaches that a lender must return a poor borrower's collateral even if he took it without בית דין's permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You shall surely return.' From this alone I would only know the case where he took the collateral with בית דין's permission. How do we know the case where he took it without בית דין's permission? The verse says 'השב תשיב', meaning in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the third example in the ברייתא. It uses the doubled verb about returning a poor person's משכון (collateral). More examples follow in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic case is a lender who took a משכון the proper way, through בית דין. We might have thought the duty to return it each night applies only then. The doubled 'השב תשיב' widens the duty: even a lender who took it on his own, without permission, must still return it.

keyTerms.meaning: You shall surely return (a doubled verb)
With the permission of the court
Collateral (an item taken to secure a loan)

steps.whatToRemember: In each case so far, the doubled verb teaches 'מכל מקום,' that the law applies in any case. Sometimes that means a different method (מות יומת, הכה תכה), and sometimes a different situation (השב תשיב).

phrases.english: 'You shall surely return,'
I have only where he took collateral from him
with the court's permission.

phrases.aramaic: מִשְׁכְּנוֹ שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת בֵּית דִּין, מִנַּיִן?
phrases.english: If he took collateral without the court's permission, from where do we know?
The verse says: 'You shall surely return,'
in any case.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״הָשֵׁב תָּשִׁיב״, אֵין לִי אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּשְׁכְּנוֹ בִּרְשׁוּת בֵּית דִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third example in the same ברייתא, this time widening the situation rather than the method.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lender must return a poor borrower's collateral each night even if he took it without בית דין's permission, learned from 'השב תשיב'.

steps.title: Collateral taken without permission must also be returned
steps.stepSummary: The doubled verb 'חבל תחבל' teaches that the lender must return the poor man's garment even if he took it without permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If you take as collateral (חבל תחבל).' From this I would only know the case where he took the collateral with permission. How do I know the case where he took it without permission? The verse says 'חבל תחבל': in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives another doubled verb, this time from the collateral verse in שמות. It teaches that the duty to return the garment applies even when the collateral was taken without permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic case is a lender who took collateral properly, with בית דין's permission. The doubling stretches the duty to return the garment to a lender who took it improperly. This sounds just like the 'השב תשיב' rule in the previous step, which sets up the גמרא's next question.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You shall surely take collateral', a doubled verb
In any case, no matter what

phrases.english: "If you take as collateral" (doubled verb),
I would only know where he took collateral with permission.
phrases.notes: 'Permission' here means with the approval of בית דין.

phrases.english: If he took collateral without permission, from where do we know?
The verse says: "חבל תחבל,"
to teach: in any case.

steps.triggerLanguage: חָבֹל תַּחְבֹּל אֵין לִי אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּשְׁכְּנוֹ בִּרְשׁוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's list of doubled verbs, with a rule that matches the one in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lender must return the poor borrower's garment even if he took it as collateral without permission.

steps.title: Why do we need two verses about returning collateral?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the תורה needs both 'השב תשיב' and 'חבל תחבל', since both seem to teach the same rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And these two verses, why do I need them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that two verses teach the same rule about returning collateral, and asks why both are needed. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both 'השב תשיב' in step 4 and 'חבל תחבל' in step 5 teach that collateral is returned even if it was taken without permission. The תורה does not write extra verses for nothing, so each verse must teach something of its own.

phrases.english: And these two verses, why do I need them?
phrases.notes: The two verses are 'השב תשיב' (דברים 24:13, from step 4) and 'חבל תחבל' (שמות 22:25).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי תְּרֵי קְרָאֵי לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the rule of step 5 is needed in addition to step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does each of the two collateral verses add?

steps.title: One verse is for a day garment, one for a night garment
steps.stepSummary: One verse covers clothing used during the day, and the other covers clothing used at night.
steps.simpleTranslation: One is for a daytime garment, and one is for a nighttime garment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that each verse covers a different kind of garment: one worn by day and one used at night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since each verse covers a different item, neither one is extra. The lender must return a day garment for the daytime and a night garment for the night, whenever the borrower needs it.

keyTerms.meaning: A garment worn during the day
A garment used at night (like a blanket)

steps.whatToRemember: The two collateral verses are both needed: one covers day clothing and the other covers night clothing.

phrases.english: One is for a daytime garment,
and one is for a nighttime garment.

steps.triggerLanguage: חַד לִכְסוּת יוֹם וְחַד לִכְסוּת לַיְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each verse covers a different garment: one for the day and one for the night.

steps.title: צדקה also goes to the poor of other cities
steps.stepSummary: The doubled verb 'פתח תפתח' teaches that the מצוה of צדקה includes poor people from another city.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You shall surely open (פתח תפתח) your hand.' From this I would only know the poor of your own city. How do I know the poor of another city? The verse says 'פתח תפתח': in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא goes back to its list of doubled verbs, now in the area of צדקה. It teaches that the duty to give also covers poor people from other cities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic case is the poor of your own town. The doubling widens the מצוה to include the poor of a different town.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You shall surely open (your hand)', a doubled verb about צדקה
The poor of your own city

phrases.english: "You shall surely open" (your hand),
I would only know about the poor of your city.
For the poor of another city, from where do we know?
The verse says: "פתח תפתח,"
to teach: in any case.

steps.triggerLanguage: פָּתֹחַ תִּפְתַּח אֵין לִי אֶלָּא לַעֲנִיֵּי עִירֶךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא's list of doubled verbs after the side question.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מצוה of צדקה includes the poor of other cities.

steps.title: Even a small gift counts as צדקה
steps.stepSummary: The doubled verb 'נתן תתן' teaches that the מצוה of giving includes a small gift, not only a large one.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You shall surely give (נתן תתן).' From this I would only know a large gift. How do I know a small gift? The verse says 'נתן תתן': in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives one more doubled verb about צדקה. It teaches that even a small gift fulfills the מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the doubling, we might think the verse only speaks about a big gift. The doubled verb includes a small gift too.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You shall surely give', a doubled verb about צדקה

steps.whatToRemember: Every doubled verb in this ברייתא follows the same pattern: the plain verse gives the basic case, and the doubling adds 'in any case' to widen the rule.

phrases.english: "You shall surely give,"
I would only know about a large gift.
A small gift, from where do we know?
The verse says: "נתן תתן,"
to teach: in any case.

steps.triggerLanguage: נָתֹן תִּתֵּן אֵין לִי אֶלָּא מַתָּנָה מְרוּבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another צדקה example to the ברייתא's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מצוה of צדקה is fulfilled even with a small gift.

steps.title: Gifts to a freed slave even when the house was not blessed
steps.stepSummary: The doubled verb 'הענק תעניק' teaches that a freed עבד עברי receives parting gifts even if his master's household did not prosper because of him.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You shall surely give him gifts.' From the end of the verse I would only know that we give gifts when the house was blessed because of him. How do we know we give gifts even when the house was not blessed because of him? The verse says 'הענק תעניק', meaning in every case.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives another example of a doubled verb, this time about the gifts a master gives his Hebrew slave when he goes free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse ends with 'what ה׳ your God has blessed you with,' which sounds like gifts are only due if the master was blessed through the slave. The extra word 'תעניק' widens the rule so the slave gets gifts in every case.

keyTerms.meaning: You shall surely give him gifts: the parting gifts for a freed Hebrew slave
The gift given to an עבד עברי when he goes free
The house was blessed because of him: the master did well thanks to the slave
In every case, no matter what

phrases.english: 'You shall surely furnish him'
I would only know
that when the house was blessed because of him, we give him gifts.
phrases.notes: This comes from the end of the same פסוק: 'of what ה׳ your God has blessed you.'

phrases.english: If the house was not blessed because of him, how do we know?
The verse teaches: 'You shall surely furnish him,'
in every case.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵךְ הַבַּיִת בִּגְלָלוֹ מַעֲנִיקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another item in the running list of doubled verbs that teach something extra.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A freed עבד עברי receives gifts whether or not the master's house was blessed because of him.

steps.title: How does רבי אלעזר בן עזריה explain the doubled verb?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה holds that gifts are given only if the house was blessed through the slave. So what does he do with the extra word 'תעניק'?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, who says: if the house was blessed because of him, we give him gifts, and if the house was not blessed because of him, we do not give gifts, why do I need the word 'תעניק'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about a תנא who disagrees with the rule just learned. If he doesn't learn 'every case' from the doubled verb, why is it written twice?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule in step 10 depended on reading the doubled verb as adding something. רבי אלעזר בן עזריה does not accept that added rule, so the extra word seems to have no job for him. This question sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who limits the gifts to a case where the master was blessed through the slave
Why do I need it? Asks what job a word in the text is doing

phrases.english: And according to רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, who says:
if the house was blessed because of him, we give him gifts;

phrases.aramaic: לֹא נִתְבָּרֵךְ הַבַּיִת בִּגְלָלוֹ – אֵין מַעֲנִיקִין,
phrases.english: if the house was not blessed because of him, we do not give gifts,
why do I need the extra word 'תעניק'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה דְּאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how a disagreeing תנא explains the doubled verb that step 10 used.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What purpose the doubled verb serves for רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, who does not learn 'every case' from it.

steps.title: The תורה speaks the way people speak
steps.stepSummary: For רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, the doubled verb is just a normal way of speaking, and nothing is learned from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תורה spoke in the language of people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי אלעזר בן עזריה does not learn anything from the doubling, because people commonly speak this way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Doubling a verb for emphasis was ordinary speech. The תורה used ordinary speech here, so the second word is not an extra hint to learn a new rule from.

keyTerms.meaning: The תורה spoke in the language of people; a doubled word may just be normal speech

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the תורה has wasted words. It means that for this תנא, this kind of doubling is a normal style of speaking and not a source for a new rule.
steps.whyThisMatters: This principle is a key disagreement: some תנאים learn from every doubled word, and others say a doubled word can just be normal speech.

phrases.english: The Torah spoke in the language of people.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּבְּרָה תוֹרָה כִּלְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The doubled verb is ordinary speech, so רבי אלעזר בן עזריה learns nothing extra from it.

steps.title: Lending even to a poor man who has money but won't use it
steps.stepSummary: The doubled verb 'העבט תעביטנו' teaches that we lend even to a person who has his own resources but does not want to live off them.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You shall surely lend him.' I would only know about someone who has nothing and doesn't want to be supported by צדקה: the תורה says give it to him as a loan. If he has money and doesn't want to support himself with it, how do we know? The verse says 'תעביטנו', meaning in every case.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives another doubled verb, this time about lending to a poor person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain verse covers a poor man with nothing who is too proud to take צדקה, so we give it to him as a loan. The extra word 'תעביטנו' adds a man who does have money but won't spend it on himself: we still lend to him.

keyTerms.meaning: To be supported or to support oneself
In the form of a loan
The Merciful One: a name for ה׳ when quoting the תורה

steps.confusionAlert: 'להתפרנס' means something slightly different in the two cases. A man with nothing won't take צדקה. A man with money won't use his own money on himself.

phrases.english: 'You shall surely lend him'
I would only know about one who has nothing
and does not want to be supported,
phrases.notes: He means he doesn't want to take צדקה.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַחֲמָנָא: תֵּן לוֹ דֶּרֶךְ הַלְוָאָה.
phrases.english: the Merciful One says: give it to him as a loan.

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ לוֹ וְאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לְהִתְפַּרְנֵס, מִנַּיִן?
phrases.english: If he has money and does not want to support himself, how do we know?
The verse teaches: 'תעביטנו,' in every case.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין לוֹ וְאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לְהִתְפַּרְנֵס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next doubled verb in the list, following the same pattern as step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We must lend even to someone who has money but refuses to use it for himself.

steps.title: How does רבי שמעון explain the doubled verb?
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון holds we don't need to help someone who has money but won't use it. So why does the תורה double the verb?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי שמעון, who says that if he has money and doesn't want to support himself, we don't need to take care of him, why do I need 'תעביטנו'?
steps.whatsHappening: Just like with רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, the גמרא asks how a disagreeing תנא explains the doubled verb.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון rejects the rule from step 13, so the extra word seems to have no job for him. This sets up the same answer as before.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who says we need not help someone who has money but won't use it
We do not need to take care of him

phrases.english: And according to רבי שמעון, who says:
if he has money and does not want to support himself,
we do not need to take care of him,
why do I need the extra word 'תעביטנו'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן דְּאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how a disagreeing תנא explains the doubled verb used in step 13, just like step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What purpose the doubled verb serves for רבי שמעון, who does not accept the rule from step 13.

steps.title: Again: the תורה speaks the way people speak
steps.stepSummary: For רבי שמעון too, the doubled verb is just normal speech and teaches nothing extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תורה spoke in the language of people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same answer as in step 12: רבי שמעון treats the doubling as ordinary speech.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern repeats exactly. Whoever disagrees with the rule learned from a doubled verb explains the doubling as the normal way people talk.

keyTerms.meaning: A doubled word, like העבט תעביטנו

steps.whatToRemember: Each doubled verb (השב תשיב, חבל תחבל, פתח תפתח, נתן תתן, הענק תעניק, העבט תעביטנו) can teach an extra rule. But a תנא who disagrees with that rule can say the doubling is just how people talk: דברה תורה כלשון בני אדם.

phrases.english: The Torah spoke in the language of people.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּבְּרָה תוֹרָה כִּלְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 14 with the same principle used in step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The doubled verb is ordinary speech, so רבי שמעון learns nothing extra from it.

steps.title: The finder cannot demand his full lost wage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: a finder who lost a סלע of work cannot demand a full סלע. He is paid like a worker instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the finder lost a סלע's worth of work, he can't say 'Give me a סלע.' Instead, the owner pays him a worker's wage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה so that it can discuss it. This line sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Returning a lost item can pull a person away from his paying job. The משנה says he does not get back the full amount he would have earned. He gets a reduced 'worker's' payment, and the next steps explain how that amount is figured.

phrases.english: If he was idle from a sela,
phrases.notes: The finder stopped a job that would have paid him a סלע, so he could look after the lost item.

phrases.english: he shall not say to him, "Give me a sela,"
rather, he gives him his wage as a laborer (idle).
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets is in the printed גמרא, but the corrected text leaves it out. Our משנה just says 'like a worker.'

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה בָּטֵל מִן הַסֶּלַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of doubled verbs and returns to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The finder gets a worker's wage, not his full lost earnings.

steps.title: Another teaching adds the word 'idle'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites a teaching that spells out the payment as 'like an idle worker.'
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: he gives him his wage like an idle worker.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a more detailed wording of the same rule. This sets up the question in the next step about what 'idle worker' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said only 'like a worker.' This teaching adds the word 'idle,' which is surprising because the finder was actually busy returning the item. That extra word is what the גמרא is about to ask about.

phrases.english: We learned:
He gives him his wage as an idle laborer.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a fuller version of the rule from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wage is measured as that of an 'idle worker.'

steps.title: What does 'idle worker' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what it means to be paid like an 'idle worker.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'like an idle worker' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for an explanation of the phrase 'idle worker.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The finder was not idle. He was working to return the item. So it is unclear what kind of 'idle' payment is meant and how much it should be.

phrases.english: What is "as an idle laborer"?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי כְּפוֹעֵל בָּטֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the wording just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the 'idle worker' payment is calculated.

steps.title: אביי: idle from his own kind of work
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the finder is paid like someone who is idle from the specific job he gave up.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: like a worker who is idle from that same kind of work he stopped doing.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question and explains what 'idle worker' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The payment depends on the job the finder left. It is the amount a person in that line of work would accept to stop his job and spend the time returning the lost item instead. So it is less than his full wage, but it still depends on what his work was.
steps.whatToRemember: The finder does not get his full lost wage. He gets what someone in his own line of work would accept to stop that work.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
As an idle laborer of that particular work,
from which he was kept idle.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about 'idle worker.'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The finder is paid what someone in his specific job would accept to stop that job for this task.

steps.title: Setting a condition in front of a בית דין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: if a בית דין is there, the finder can set a condition in front of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there is a בית דין there, he can set a condition in front of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה. This sets up the story that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually the finder gets only the reduced 'idle worker' wage. But if he states his terms in front of a בית דין, he can make sure he receives his full lost wage.

phrases.english: If there is a court there –
he may stipulate before them.
phrases.notes: The finder can say in front of them that he'll return the item only if he gets his full lost wage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם יֵשׁ שָׁם בֵּית דִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A condition made in front of a בית דין lets the finder claim his full lost wage.

steps.title: רב ספרא splits from איסור in front of two people
steps.stepSummary: איסור and רב ספרא were business partners. רב ספרא ended the partnership without איסור knowing, with only two people present.
steps.simpleTranslation: איסור and רב ספרא had a business partnership. רב ספרא went and split it up without איסור knowing, in front of two people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story about doing something in front of a בית דין. It sets up the ruling that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ספרא wanted to end the partnership while his partner was away. He did it in front of only two people, not three. That raises the question of whether two people are enough to act as a court.

phrases.english: Issur and Rav Safra
made a joint venture with each other.
Rav Safra went and divided it
without Issur's knowledge
in the presence of two.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיסּוּר וְרַב סָפְרָא עֲבֻיד עִיסְקָא בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells a story connected to acting in front of a בית דין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: a partnership was split up in front of only two people.

steps.title: רבה בר רב הונא asks for three people
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא came before רבה בר רב הונא, who told him to bring the three people he split the partnership in front of, or another option.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came before רבה בר רב הונא, who told him: Go bring the three people you split it in front of. Or else...
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר רב הונא gives his ruling: splitting the partnership needs three people, like a court. He then begins to offer another option.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two people were not enough. Acting for someone who is not there requires a בית דין of three, which matches the משנה's 'if there is a בית דין there.' The words 'or else' begin a second option that continues past this point.

phrases.aramaic: אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא,
phrases.english: He came before Rabba bar Rav Huna,
He said to him: Go bring
three before whom you divided it,
or alternatively

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling on רב ספרא's action.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Acting for an absent partner requires three people, like a בית דין, not just two.
